items.s: Last night she ____ a long message to her teacher.

tfn.s: Experts suggest beginning with a very small part of the task.
tfn.why: The text says: "Experts often suggest starting small."

tfn.s: The 2026 studies showed connections rather than proof of a cause.
tfn.why: The text says: "These studies showed connections, not proof that one problem always causes another."

tfn.s: Procrastination is more common among younger people than older people.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not compare younger and older people.

tfn.s: Recent studies suggest that procrastination is simply laziness.
tfn.why: The text says the opposite: "One common explanation is that people are simply lazy, but recent studies suggest a more complicated picture."

tfn.s: The writer says it is better to wait until you feel ready before you begin.
tfn.why: The text says: "It also helps to stop waiting until you feel completely ready."

focus.note: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word. The small word changes the meaning, so learn them together, such as give up.

tfn.s: Procrastination is more common in students than in people at work.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not compare students with people at work.

tfn.s: The research proves that phones cause procrastination.
tfn.why: The text says it "cannot establish that phones or perfectionism directly cause procrastination".

tfn.s: According to the text, avoiding a task can bring short relief that disappears later.
tfn.why: The text says avoiding it offers relief, "even if that relief disappears when the deadline approaches".

tfn.s: A person who writes a rough first draft may be in a better position than a perfectionist.
tfn.why: The text says someone willing to write a rough draft "may have a useful starting point", while the perfectionist has nothing on the page.

tfn.s: The writer says blaming yourself is the best way to deal with procrastination.
tfn.why: The text says "blaming yourself for being lazy may miss the point".

focus.note: Some phrasal verbs have three parts, such as come up with. The verb changes with the tense, but the small words stay the same.

tfn.s: The writer suggests that procrastination can sometimes reflect too much concern rather than too little.
tfn.why: The text says it is "not necessarily an absence of concern; sometimes it is concern becoming so uncomfortable that we struggle to act".

tfn.s: The Italian study found that people who procrastinate more did worse on every task measuring attention.
tfn.why: The text says they did less well on "some of those tasks", not all of them.

tfn.s: The writer believes a short timer works better than breaking a task into small actions.
tfn.why: The text recommends both but never compares them.

tfn.s: The writer accepts that the suggested strategies may not fully overcome anxiety or attention difficulties.
tfn.why: The text says such strategies "do not remove every psychological obstacle, particularly where anxiety or attention difficulties are significant".

tfn.s: The writer's aim is to help people turn every minute into productivity.
tfn.why: The text says "The goal is not to turn every minute into productivity".

speak.title: Role-play: the report nobody wants to start
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.role: the colleague who wants to start now
a.text: You and your colleague must finish a report by Friday. You want to start today, even with a small part. Explain why starting early helps and suggest a first step.

b.role: the colleague who wants to wait
b.text: You'd rather wait until you feel ready. Explain why. Listen to your colleague's plan and decide if you can agree on a small first step.

phrases: I think we should start today.
I'd rather wait until I feel ready.
Let's just write the first heading.
That's a fair point, but I'm not in the mood.
How about fifteen minutes with our phones away?
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class what you agreed and whether it was a good plan.
